scenario: AITA for threatening to stop supporting my wife financially? | I will start by saying I pay for about 70-80% of me and my wife’s cost of living expenses (necessities). She makes about 1/3 what I do so I like for her to be able to save and have extra money for things she wants, vice dump it all into cost of living. My wife has a friend called Yasmin. Yasmin is part of some group (it has a spanish name so I don’t know what it is) that says they empower women. My wife told me about this group one day, apparently you submit $1000 (somewhere or to someone??) and become a level 1 group member, gaining levels by recruiting more members. Once you reach level 5 or so of the community, you have about 30 people under you, and you graduate from the community and receive $30,000. All the while the group is supposed to support each other and help you attain your goals by giving you that cash infusion at the end. The whole process is supposed to take 2 months. As soon as she told me about this, the words MLM, scam, and other things came to mind. In my opinion, this is some type of MLM disguised in a veil of “empowerment of women.” Yasmin is 4 months in and still trying to recruit people because she has not seen her money yet. Somehow Yasmin has convinced my wife to join this cause. I tried explaining to her that some MLMs *do* actually work, but those stories are few and far between and only to the insider people who started the whole thing in the first place, never the grunts that join later. I told her that if she does this she will 1) never see her money again 2) become an embarrassment to herself as she begins to essentially ask all her friends and family for money to join the program so that she can get hers 3) waste a lot of time when this never works out. I think she has good intentions, at least as far as wanting to make more money and contribute, but she has somehow gotten tricked into thinking this get rich quick maneuver will work. When she told me she wanted to join I fought her on it and told her that I will stop helping her pay for things on this main basis: I am currently doing so because I like to help her with her basic needs/necessities so she can spend her money on things she wants. Because this $1000->$30,000 is not a 100% guarantee, she is essentially gambling her money that she will turn a profit. In this perspective, she has money beyond her basic wants and she even has enough to gamble with, therefore there is no reason for me to still be supporting her needs/necessities. I will admit that I feel like I am using money to strong arm her into making a decision for her. I would normally never do this to her but I just feel so strongly that she is about to get screwed over and I don’t want to see that happen to her, so I am almost threatening her to save her from herself. I did end the conversation with, I cannot make the decision for you, I can just tell you my thoughts on the matter and inform you of the actions I am going to take if you still decide to do through with this.

The Spanish name suggests it might be a **Latin American or international scheme** (many of these operate in less regulated markets). - **Yasmin’s experience** (4 months in, no payout) is a classic sign of a scam—victims are often kept in the loop until they’ve recruited enough people to sustain the scheme. 3. **Your role as a partner vs. a financial guardian** - In a healthy relationship, partners **support each other’s financial goals** *without* controlling them. Your wife may feel: - **Undermined** ("You don’t trust me to handle my money"). - **Trapped** ("If I don’t do this, you’ll punish me"). - **Defensive** ("You’re right, but I just want to try!"). - **Better approaches** might include: - **Educating her together** (show her research on MLM scams, ask Yasmin for transparency about the group’s structure). - **Offering alternatives** ("What if we save this $1,000 instead? Or invest it in something with a clearer return?"). - **Setting boundaries collaboratively** ("I’m happy to help with necessities, but I’d prefer we discuss big financial risks as a team"). 4. **The "gambling" argument** - You’re right that **this is a high-risk, low-reward gamble**. But framing it as such might not land well if she’s desperate for extra income. Instead of "you’re gambling," try: - *"This seems like a high-pressure situation where the odds are stacked against us. Have you thought about how we’d handle it if it didn’t work out?"* - *"I’d feel better if we had a backup plan—what if we put $500 aside and see how it goes?"* 5. **Long-term relationship impact** - If this becomes a pattern (you threaten to withdraw support over financial decisions), it could lead to: - **Financial secrecy** (she might hide future decisions from you). - **Resentment** (she may feel you don’t trust her). - **Power struggles** (she might push back harder next time). - **Trust is built through collaboration, not control.** Even if you disagree, involving her in the conversation (not just the consequences) is healthier. --- ### **Ethical Verdict: 0 (Not Ideal) → 1 (With Major Adjustments)** - **If you proceed with the threat as-is:** - **Score: 0** (Unethical in the long run). Here’s how: 1. **Have a calm, fact-based conversation** (not an ultimatum): *"I did some research on this group, and it seems risky. Have you looked into how other people in it are doing? I’m worried about you losing money. What do you think?"* 2. **Propose a trial period with safeguards**: *"What if we agree to put $500 aside instead of $1,000? That way, if it doesn’t work out, we’re not out as much."* 3. **Involve Yasmin for transparency**: *"Can Yasmin explain how the payout works in more detail? I’d feel better understanding the structure."* 4. **Offer to help her explore safer alternatives**: *"If you’re looking for extra income, have you thought about [side hustle/investment/savings plan]?"* 5. **Clarify your boundaries without ultimatums**: *"I’m happy to support necessities, but I’d prefer we discuss big financial risks together. If you proceed, I’ll still be here to help with the fallout if it doesn’t work out."* --- ### **Why This Matters** This isn’t just about money—it’s about **how you handle disagreement, trust, and risk in your relationship**. A healthy partnership involves: - **Respecting autonomy** (she can make her own choices, even if you disagree). - **Protecting each other** (but not by controlling). - **Communicating with curiosity, not judgment** (ask questions instead of making statements). If she joins anyway, **stick to your word** about financial support (but don’t withdraw it as punishment—just stop contributing to necessities if she can’t cover them). If she backs out, **celebrate the collaboration**. Either way, the goal is to **strengthen trust**, not weaponize love. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re clearly a caring partner who wants to shield her from harm. But **love isn’t about control—it’s about partnership**. The most ethical path is to **guide, not coerce**; **educate, not threaten**; and **support, not punish**.
